extracted.intended_audience: students of journalism and practicing newspaper reporters learning how to write news stories
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and examples on composing news pieces (straight reporting and human-interest features), showing how to bring out human interest in routine dispatches and how to use documents, quotes, figures, and local angles. Uses real newspaper examples (patent award, adoption, wills, receivership) to illustrate techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bring out human interest in routine news
rubrics_metrics.description: “The way in which the human interest can be brought out in what might ordinarily be considered routine news, is shown by the second of the following two stories.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use personal detail, scene-setting, and emotional reactions to transform routine factual items into human-interest pieces. Example: contrast the straight Patent-Office report with the Evening World humanized portrait of Janin — his shop scene, his family, his reaction. The textbook illustrates that the same core fact (patent award) can be handled as dry official news or as a human story by adding color, dialogue, and personal hopes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose appropriate tone: straight report vs human-interest feature
rubrics_metrics.description: Implicit throughout the paired examples (NY Times factual account vs Evening World profile) is the principle of selecting tone and structure appropriate to the story purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For authoritative, concise facts (legal decisions, financial transactions) adopt a straight-news tone with emphasis on official statements and documentary facts. For feature treatment, emphasize character, atmosphere, quotes, and prospects (what the result means to people). The same event can be reworked according to audience and paper style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use specific figures and concrete particulars
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories routinely include precise dollar amounts, dates, percentages, and counts (e.g., $2,500,000 held by banks; $1,000,000 preferred stock; $600,000 cash on hand; bequests of $500, $1,500, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include exact numbers, dates, and quantified details to lend authority and clarity. Precise figures make the scale and stakes of a story comprehensible to readers and support claims about consequences (losses, liabilities, bequests).

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide background and chronological context
rubrics_metrics.description: Narratives supply prior events and sequence (e.g., issuance of preferred stock, auditors discovering discrepancies, earlier panics that reduced trade) to explain why current developments occurred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report the events leading up to the main action so readers understand causes and likely outcomes. Use chronology to connect immediate events (receivership, assignment, probate) with underlying trends (market panic, past consolidations, prior illnesses).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use direct quotations and attributable statements
rubrics_metrics.description: The excerpts quote principals (e.g., Mr. Arthur, Receiver Harrison, Janin, Mrs. Janin, judges, attorneys) to convey perspective and authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include salient direct quotes with clear attribution to reveal motives, color, and emotion, and to document official positions. Quotations can humanize subjects and provide evidentiary support for reported claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit documents and official records as reporting sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories rely on documents and formal actions (patent office findings, deed of assignment, will admitted to probate, court orders voiding an adoption) as primary evidentiary bases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report the contents and legal import of documents and court actions; quote or summarize key provisions (e.g., bequests, probate terms) and note procedural effects (rights, orders, admissions to probate). Documents supply authoritative facts and quotations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Localize national stories by finding local hooks
rubrics_metrics.description: Note: “The provision in the will given in the New York court story making bequests to Chicago nurses, formed the basis of the local story in the Chicago paper; both stories follow.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and emphasize elements of a larger story that have local relevance (names, bequests to local residents, ties to local institutions) to create follow-up or localized versions for different papers/audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report legal/procedural outcomes and practical consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: The examples report concrete legal and practical results (assignment for benefit of creditors, appointment of receiver, ancillary receivers, probate admissions, court voiding adoption).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make clear the official outcome and its practical implications (who controls assets, who may reclaim property, financial shortfalls, prospective liabilities). Explain what will happen next (funding needs, litigation, distribution schedules) so readers grasp consequences.
